# Theoretical background and problem setting

Following the spirit of @ehrhardt2021rejectReview, I begin by formally
presenting the Reject Inference Problem in Credit Risk as understood and
approached in this thesis, so that the hypothesis formulation and the
theoretical properties of the proposed solution can be precisely formulated.
First and also following the approach of @ehrhardt2021rejectReview a detailed
description in natural language of the biasing mechanism in FIs is done, so
that each concept used can be defined properly avoiding confusions. Second a
measure theoretic characterization of the biasing process through its assumed
underlying random variables is given. Finally a characterization of the available
data for the FI is done as observed realizations of this process and its random
variables. Although the main focus of this thesis is not bettering the formalization
approaches, I find it important to be thorough so that future work can properly
criticise this thesis.

## Concepts definition

When a financial institution (FI) is going to grant a credit, it has recieven
first some information related to an applicant. This information is constituted
by the features, which are then used in a scoring model ("model features") and
other characteristics e. g. whether the applicant dresses well in a face to face
application. Based on the recieved information the FI decides whether to approve
the loan. Almost always this decision will be dependent on a scorecard, which
based on some encodable characteristics of the applicant returns a score. These
characteristics will be called "model features". On FI's approval a financing
contract can be concluded leading to disbursement.  A credit-agreement after
drawdown is called here "accepted".^[As both parties accepted for the contract
to be concluded] If an application does not lead to the FI's payout, it is called
"rejected".^[Note that no differentiation on whether rejection came from the FI or
the applicant is made]

<!-- Download LTeX for language corrections -->

If an accepted applicant pays back (on time/in full - depending on the FI's
definition) its credit as per constract is considered to be a non-default, a good
loan, otherwise it is seen as a default. Whether an applicant will default or not
can be considered as a random outcome depending on its characteristics and maybe
some exogenous factors which can be seen as "noise" affecting the random variable.
In this sense, if we ignore the noise, an applicant can be seen as either a defaulter
or a payer if we assume the payment outcome to be some (measurable) function of its
features. In some sense can then be seen "is a payer" as a characteristic of the
applicant that "gets realized at the same time as its features". See that this does
not mean that an FI could have "a perfect model" - as this factors determining
whether an applicant will default are not (realistically) fully known to an FI
neither the dependence structure. All non-exogenous information which conditions
the payment outcome of the applicant that is not included in the model
features is called "hidden features".

## Measure theoretic description

Let $X_m, X_h, Y, Y_m, Z, \epsilon$ and $\varepsilon$ be random variables on the
probability space $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})$. Define with $f_o, f_i \in \mathbb{N}$
$$
X_o: (\Omega, \mathcal{F}) \to \left(\mathbb{R}^{f_o}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^{f_o}) \right), \quad
X_h: (\Omega, \mathcal{F}) \to \left(\mathbb{R}^{f_h}, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^{f_h}) \right)
$$

as the random variables generating the applicant's model and hidden features. The joint distribution of both features sets is characterized by
$$
X : (\Omega, \mathcal{F}) \to \left(\mathbb{R}^{f}, \mathcal{B}\left(\mathbb{R}^{f} \right) \right), f:=f_m + f_h
$$
with
$$
\forall \omega \in \Omega: X(\omega) := \begin{pmatrix} X_m(\omega) \\ X_h(\omega) \end{pmatrix}
$$
Further with $V$ a placeholder for $Y, Z$ and $Y_m$ let
$$
V : (\Omega, \mathcal{F}) \to \left( E_V, 2^{E_V} \right)
$$
with
$$
E_Y = \{g,b\}, \quad E_Z = \{a,r\}, \quad E_{Y_m} = \{g,b, \texttt{na}\}
$$

be the random variables describing the repayment type, acceptance decision and observable repayment outcome of the loan applied for defined $\forall \omega \in \Omega$ as
$$
Y(\omega) = \begin{cases}
    b & \text{if applicant is a defaulter} \\
    g & \text{if applicant is a payer}
\end{cases} ,
$$
$$
Z(\omega) = \begin{cases}
    a & \text{if applicant gets accepted (financed)} \\
    r & \text{if applicant gets rejected (non-financed)}
\end{cases}
$$
and
$$
Y_m(\omega) = \begin{cases}
    Y(\omega) & Z(\omega) = a \\
    \texttt{na} & Z(\omega) = r
\end{cases}
$$

$Z$ is more precisely modeled as a measurable function of both features sets. Let
$$
s : \mathbb{R}^{f_m} \to \mathbb{R}, \; 
\mathcal{B}\left(\mathbb{R}^{f_m}\right)-\mathcal{B}\left(\mathbb{R}\right) \text{ measurable}
$$
be a score function and
$$
d : \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}^{f_h} \to \{a, r\}, \;
    \left(\mathcal{B}\left(\mathbb{R}\right)
    \otimes
    \mathcal{B}\left(\mathbb{R}^{f_m}\right)\right) - 2^{\{a, r\}}
    \text{ measurable}
$$

an acceptance decision function. Then

$$
\forall \omega \in \Omega: \:
Z(\omega) =
d\left(
    s\left(X_m(\omega)\right),
    X_h(\omega)
\right)
$$

Consider thereby that this form does not imply that $d$ "reacts" to every
component from $X_h$, i. e. a subsset of hidden features can (and realistically
will) be independent from $Z$. In this spirit, $Y$ can also be modeled as
$$
$\forall \omega \in \Omega:
Y(\omega) = \begin{cases}
    \varepsilon(\omega) & \epsilon(\omega) = \text{external effect} \\
    \iota \left(X_m(\omega), X_h(\omega) \right) & \epsilon(\omega) = \text{no external effect}
\end{cases}
$$

with
$$
\epsilon(\omega) : (\Omega, \mathcal{F}) \to \left(E_\epsilon, 2^{E_\epsilon} \right), \quad
\varepsilon(\omega) : (\Omega, \mathcal{F}) \to \left(E_Y, 2^{E_Y} \right)
$$

the random variables defining whether an external effect overrides the "usual behavior"
and what the external effect ends up causing (e. g. if there is a shock in the laboral
market and whether it is positive or negative for the applicant). Finally $\iota$ would
be a $\left(\mathcal{B}^{\mathbb{R^{f_m}}} \otimes \mathbb{R^{f_h}}\right)$-
$2^{E_Y}$ measurable function
